articles.body: Boeing's largest 737 Max jet has cleared a major regulatory hurdle, with US aviation authorities approving the Max 10 for passenger service on Tuesday after nearly a decade of delays. The certification marks a boost for the planemaker's recovery, with deliveries expected to begin in 2027.
articles.headline: Boeing's 737 Max 10 finally wins FAA approval after years of delays

articles.body: After implementing curfews in cities across France to prevent a continuation of the weekend's violence and looting, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu prepared to meet with trade union organisations on Wednesday to discuss protest security and responses to the high school students who began the now nationwide protests. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
articles.headline: Live: French PM Lecornu to meet with unions ahead of new protests

articles.body: Italy announced tougher security measures on Tuesday after weekend riots in Milan left more than 100 police officers injured and shops looted. The government will deploy 500 additional soldiers, impose harsher penalties for violent protesters and hold parents financially responsible for damage caused by minors.
articles.headline: Italy announces new security measures after Milan riots, deploying 500 soldiers

articles.body: Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in Africa's latest outbreak, while Kenya reported its ninth infection, raising fears of further spread across the continent. Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya warned of an “extremely serious threat” and urged the international community to send funding, medical supplies and health workers.
articles.headline: Nigeria records first Ebola case as outbreak spreads across Africa

articles.body: Two weeks out from the Midterm elections, there’s bipartisan pushback against data centers that suck the water and power out of communities. Just two years ago, ChatGPT was still a brand new thing, and AI was admired with awe by most voters. Like in 2024, the hot button issue in swing constituencies remains inflation or ‘the price of eggs’. But anxiety over the end of the month is now coupled with anxiety over the end of the world. In 2026, bots and large language models write papers and churn out campaign ads. We'll ask about calls for regulation despite fierce resistance from tech billionaires and whether the latest wobbles from the stock market signal that the race to corner the market and scale up at warp speed may be running out of road.
articles.headline: AI on the ballot? Voters in US midterms revolt against data centres

articles.body: In tonight's programme, Nigeria confirms its first Ebola case in the midst of an outbreak that began in DRC Congo in mid-May. Also, a former top South African police officer facing sexual grooming and rape charges is denied bail. Finally, São Tomé and Príncipe's rich volcanic soils produce vanilla pods with an entrancing taste unlike those grown anywhere else.
articles.headline: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case

articles.body: Egypt's parliament on Monday delayed a debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia until next week, state media reported, after an emergency session ended without a decision a day earlier. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Dr May Darwich, Associate Professor in International Relations of the Middle East at the University of Birmingham. She explains that "this kind of military operation does not really have any objectives or exit strategy so at the moment this might actually weaken Egypt's regional role".
articles.headline: Egypt involvement in Yemen 'may actually weaken Cairo's regional role', expert says

articles.body: Paris Saint-Germain came from behind to beat Barcelona 4-2 in a Champions League thriller on Tuesday, handing the Catalans their first defeat of the season. Liverpool staged a dramatic comeback to edge Villarreal 4-3 at Anfield, while Manchester City cruised to a 5-1 victory over AEK Athens.
articles.headline: PSG end Barcelona's winning run as Liverpool fight back against Villarreal

articles.body: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign is preparing to request the annulment of right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro's candidacy over alleged social media interference from US tech giant Meta as Brazil’s presidential race intensifies ahead of Sunday’s runoff. The petition that will be submitted to the country's top electoral court claims "algorithmic manipulation" by Meta to suppress Lula's campaign content and boost Bolsonaro.
articles.headline: Lula's campaign seeks to disqualify Bolsonoro from Brazil presidential vote over Meta 'interference'

articles.body: The US Federal Aviation Administration has given final approval for the 737-10, the largest model in Boeing's best-selling Max family. The certification comes more than five years after the narrowbody jet's maiden flight, and marks an important step for the planemaker that's been trying to regain ground following a safety and management crisis. Plus, the French government has offered all businesses affected by the recent riots a interest-free loan of up to 50,000 euros.
articles.headline: US regulators certify Boeing 737 Max 10 after years of delay

articles.body: A video showing French riot police violently beating a 26-year-old street medic in Paris has gone viral, with social media users falsely claiming he died from his injuries. But the street medic is alive, and spoke to FRANCE 24. The rumour was fuelled by confusion with a separate incident that same day: a man died of cardiac arrest in the same area, causing online users to conflate the two events. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
articles.headline: ‘I’m alive’: Paris street medic isn’t dead, despite viral claims he was killed by police

articles.body: With the midterm elections fast approaching, US President Donald Trump is stumping for candidates in states that he won by double digits in 2024. Despite what he says, it’s a sign of what Trump and the Republican party are fearing: with polls showing GOP support slip drastically even in some deep red states. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis has more.
articles.headline: Trump campaigning in Republican strongholds amid slide in polls

articles.body: Italy on Tuesday approved the deployment of 500 troops to Milan after violent clashes as fuel price protests hit pasta production and food deliveries in southern Italy. A cabinet meeting on Tuesday also approved a series of security measures, including making the detention of minors easier and introducing the crime of "violent participation in a demonstration". FRANCE 24's Seema Gupta reports from Rome.
articles.headline: Italy sends troops, toughens security laws after Milan clashes

articles.body: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Tuesday vowed a "massive" police presence at fresh protests called for the coming weekend, as he faced criticism over the handling of recent street violence. The eurozone's second-largest economy was rocked on Saturday by some of its worst rioting in recent years, just six months before voters head to the polls to elect a successor to President Emmanuel Macron. FRANCE 24's Ellen Gainsford reports.
articles.headline: French PM vows 'massive' police deployment for new demonstrations

articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu basked in Donald Trump's endorsement on Monday ahead of close-fought elections, airing a phone call in which the US president predicted he would win and suggested they may again attack Iran together. FRANCE 24's Noga Tarnopolsky reports from Jerusalem. FRANCE 24's Mark Owen speaks with Simon Mabon, Professor of International Politics and Middle East Studies at Lancaster University.
articles.headline: 'Netanyahu is fighting for his political career', expert says a week ahead of crucial vote

articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was meeting US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday in a ​bid to rescue relations that have sunk to new lows as President Donald Trump has courted Moscow and Kyiv has complained about Washington withholding vital defences. FRANCE 24's Gulliver Cragg reports from Kharkiv.
articles.headline: Zelensky meets Witkoff as US-Ukraine relations sink to new lows

articles.body: Since the 17th of October over 2,000 people have been placed in police custody in France. Nearly 70% are adults. The trials which have gotten underway help shed light on their profiles, what they did, what's the proof and what penalty they're likely to face. FRANCE 24's Delano D'Souza reports.
articles.headline: Hundreds put on immediate trial for ransacking city centres across France

articles.body: Paris police ordered a new curfew for parts of the city for Tuesday overnight, after one the previous night that authorities said resulted in calm being restored following weekend riots and looting. The fresh curfew runs from 2100 GMT Tuesday to 0400 GMT Wednesday and applies to the Republique public square in the city's central east, where many weekend clashes took place, and in the central les Halles district which is full of shops. FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago reports from central Paris.
articles.headline: New Paris curfew ordered in parts of city from 2100 GMT Tuesday

articles.body: French police are turning to social media to identify and arrest suspects linked to last weekend’s looting and unrest. Investigators are scrutinising videos posted online alongside footage from thousands of security cameras to track suspects and gather evidence. The crackdown comes as the government vows to hold those responsible for the violence and damage to shops accountable.
articles.headline: How French police are harnessing social media to identify looters

articles.body: At least 153 people have been killed in a drone strike on a market in the disputed Abyei region, where a fire at a nearby fuel depot continued to burn on Tuesday. Local officials blamed Sudan’s military for Monday’s attack, which also left dozens injured.
articles.headline: More than 150 killed in Sudan drone strike on disputed Abyei border region

articles.body: French cities that imposed a curfew Monday saw a generally calm night, after October 17 protests devolved into violent riots this past weekend. Despite criticism from citizens, France's government said it is maintaining the measure where necessary on Tuesday night.
articles.headline: France: Local curfews imposed after protests

articles.body: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome François Gouyette, former French ambassador to the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Against a backdrop of violent unrest at home and escalating conflict in the Middle East, French President Emmanuel Macron's Gulf diplomacy underscores the increasingly blurred boundaries between domestic economic security and international strategic commitments. Ambassador Gouyette argues that the visit serves a dual purpose: alleviating France's energy pressures while reaffirming its longstanding defense partnerships with Gulf monarchies. Insisting that "France has to play its role as a key partner," Gouyette portrays French military assistance as an expression of strategic solidarity rather than direct participation in the war with Iran.
articles.headline: France's decades-long ties with Gulf states built on 'economic development, oil, defence agreements'

articles.body: With US President Donald Trump’s approval rating falling to a record low of 31%, Republicans are facing mounting concerns ahead of November’s midterm elections. Republicans are at risk of losing control of the House of Representatives, but how big could the Democrats’ gains be? FRANCE 24’s International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani explains.
articles.headline: US midterm elections: Trump approval rating falls to new low

articles.body: BLAKEMAN’S (LACK OF) ENERGY PLAN: GOP gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman continued to hammer Gov. Kathy Hochul on rising energy costs today, promising to slash utility bills in half if he’s elected. The Republican, however, still has not offered up a policy proposal on how he’d go about doing that. “Kathy Hochul increased our utility rates 48 times in four years,” Blakeman said in upper Manhattan this morning. The Washington Heights press conference, which included former Gov. George Pataki, was heavy on rhetoric and relatively light on details. Afterward, Blakeman’s campaign would not spell out how exactly he plans to cut consumer utility costs and did not respond to a request for clarification about his claim that Hochul increased utility rates 48 times. (While the state’s Public Service Commission has approved increases in major utility rate cases during Hochul’s tenure, those hikes have been less than what the utilities requested .) “Donald Trump’s puppet, Bruce Blakeman … wants data centers raising your costs and said Trump was doing an ‘amazing job’ after he jacked up utility bills.” Hochul campaign spokesperson Sarafina Chitika said in a statement. “Two weeks from irrelevance, here’s what Blakeman won’t tell you: Governor Kathy Hochul delivered a billion dollars in energy relief, ten billion in tax relief, and made data centers pay for the energy they use.” The Nassau County executive described meeting the owner of a Bronx diner who told him the business would need to sell 1,000 burgers a month to pay its $16,000 utility bill. Blakeman said he would legalize fracking to help New Yorkers lower their energy bills fast. Aside from the fact that fracking doesn’t necessarily lead to lower utility bills and the reality that Blakeman would need buy-in from the state’s Democratic-dominated Legislature to do so, he insists that legalizing fracking could offer near-term relief from high energy costs. “I met with those same individuals and companies that are doing the extraction of natural gas in Pennsylvania. They told me they can be up and running in 60 days,” Blakeman said. “If Albany has the will to reduce people's utility bills … we can get it done in 60 days.” He pointed to Pennsylvania, arguing that the state has lower electric bills because it allows fracking. But he neglected to mention that Pennsylvania is not part of the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative — the carbon trading program of 11 eastern states, which Blakeman has pledged to withdraw from if he is elected. Pataki, the last Republican to serve as governor in the Empire State, spearheaded the creation of that initiative, which is commonly known as RGGI. “The concept is right, but the way it's being done in Albany is wrong,” Pataki said at the presser, accusing Albany of using RGGI as a “slush fund.” Even if New York did withdraw from RGGI, the benefit would amount to a 5% to 6% decrease on an average New York residential household bill, according to an estimate from National Grid — barely making a dent in the 50% Blakeman is promising to slash. Exactly how the state would cover the rest of his proposed cut remains unclear. Affordability, though, continues to be a key concern in Washington Heights, a largely Dominican neighborhood that Mayor Zohran Mamdani did well in during his ascent to victory last year. To drive their message home, the Republicans even attempted to make their pitch in Spanish. Pataki, much more practiced in this than Blakeman, talked about how much he loved the “barrio” when he was governor, describing Blakeman as a leader “muy fuerte.” “Gracias, hombre grande,” Blakeman exclaimed, before touting what he views as the GOP ticket’s immigrant bonafides — Saritha Komatireddy for attorney general and Joe Hernandez for comptroller. “Governor, your Spanish is better than my Spanish, and I grew up speaking it,” Hernandez praised Pataki. — Mona Zhang From the Capitol LABOR BOOSTS GOV: A coalition of public employee unions is joining the crowded roster of super PACs spending on the gubernatorial election. The New York Accountability Coalition has received $550,000 in recent weeks from the Civil Service Employees Association, Public Employees Federation, District Council 37, and CWA District One. It’ll soon spend that money to boost Hochul. The governor “is laser-focused on lowering costs for working families and investing in public services,” AFSCME’s Courtney Brunelle-Kim said. “Bruce Blakeman is just another pay-to-play politician. From now until Election Day, we’ll be working to ensure that voters in key districts know The Blakeman Record.” The super PAC spent $460,000 this spring helping Comptroller Tom DiNapoli as he faced two Democratic primary challengers. — Bill Mahoney FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL AD PULLED: A clean energy super PAC yanked a version of an ad airing in a competitive upstate House district after Republican candidate Anthony Constantino’s attorney complained the spot was defamatory. The group Invest In Tomorrow Coalition recently began airing the spot in the sprawling North Country House seat that accused Constantino — who runs a custom sticker business — of selling anti-police merchandise. “What do Anthony Constantino and violent anti-cop extremists have in common? They both think ‘kill the police’ is a good slogan,” the ad’s narrator says. Constantino’s attorney last week contacted a lawyer for the super PAC alleging the contents of the ad were false and defamatory. On Saturday, the group signaled it would suspend further distribution of the current ad. So far, the PAC has spent some $243,000 in the district in the last three days, according to AdImpact. “Anthony Constantino may lawyer up, but he can’t sticker over the truth: he’s gotten rich off selling vile merch, including hosting a listing for a ‘Kill the Police’ sticker and other anti-cop listings that are still active today ,” said Chris Coffey, a spokesperson for the group. “As a token of our gratitude and recognition of his desire to spread that message, ITC PAC is putting $250,000 more behind the original ad buy to make sure all of NY-21 knows the real Anthony Constantino.” The fight over the commercial comes as Constantino is trying to retain the seat being vacated by GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik. Polls have shown Democrat Blake Gendebien running competitively against the Republican, however, giving the race a surprising dose of uncertainty in the final two weeks. — Nick Reisman HOUSE HUNTING: Two New York battleground districts have again moved in Democrats’ favor, according to a nonpartisan election forecaster. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted Stefanik’s upstate seat from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” today, as well as Democratic Rep. Laura Gillen’s Long Island district from “leans Democratic” to “likely Democratic.” The Stefanik seat covers a sprawling, deep-red area — though Democrats are feeling bullish in part because of the Trump administration’s tariffs impacting farmers there. Gillen faces a challenge from Hempstead Receiver of Taxes Jeanine Driscoll. Kamala Harris narrowly won that district in 2024, but Republicans are counting on tailwinds from Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, to boost down-ballot candidates. — Madison Fernandez IN OTHER NEWS — REAL ESTATE STRIKES BACK: A new organization called Built For New York hopes to promote the real estate industry’s interests in the wake of a pro-tenant political sweep in New York City. ( The New York Times ) — PAC ALERT: A coalition of Jewish Democrats from the Capital Region launched a state-level PAC dedicated to supporting liberal candidates who push back on anti-Jewish and anti-Israel forces. ( Jewish Insider ) — BOOZE BUCKS: Lily Fan, chair of the State Liquor Authority and a close Hochul ally, donated $40,000 to a pro-Hochul super PAC that’s run by people who lobby the liquor industry. ( New York Focus ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

articles.body: Republicans locked in tight races this November are desperately hoping the Trump administration’s last-minute gambit to send farmers $8 billion in taxpayer money will work. President Donald Trump announced the new round of money, aimed at farmers struggling with high diesel prices, during a Monday rally for at-risk GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas. The move comes as White House officials have scrambled to address anger in farm states from Republicans. Trump’s decisions to import more foreign beef , his tariff regime and high fuel costs amid the Iran war have riled already strained farmers and ranchers — a key GOP voting bloc. Farmers won’t know how much money to expect for several more weeks. Even then, if approved, they won’t receive the payments until late November or early December at the earliest, according to three people close to the plans, granted anonymity to share details. With two weeks to go before the election, the new aid may also arrive too late to convince some voters. But top Republicans are banking on the announcement to stem GOP bleeding in farm states — especially in the Midwest, where Marshall, GOP Senate nominee Ashley Hinson in Iowa and GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Michigan have been struggling in their election campaigns. In some cases, they've broken with Trump publicly on high prices and the war. “This will go a long way to making sure the folks that feed us have it a bit easier when they most need it,” said Rep. Derrick Van Orden, referring to the farmers in his district. The Republican is locked in a highly competitive race in a rural-heavy stretch in Wisconsin’s 3rd District. However, the internal USDA taxpayer-funded account Trump is tapping for the payments doesn’t actually have enough money in it right now to make the payments, meaning Congress will have to approve the new funds or the administration will have to take it from another program, according to three Trump officials who were granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Marshall — who’s facing a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign in deep-red territory — and Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) were among the Republicans who helped push for the $8 billion, according to the three Trump officials. Marshall requested the administration allocate money to assist farmers with spiked fuel costs in a letter to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins in September. “Roger Marshall is the leader who fought for that to happen,” Trump said during the Monday rally. Spokespeople for Marshall and for Scott did not respond to requests for comment . The White House referred POLITICO to USDA’s announcement on the money. USDA spokesperson Harry Fones said in a statement that the aid package is Trump’s “latest action to deliver” for farmers and the department is actively reviewing the data to determine payments. Trump’s decision also comes after administration officials realized the president’s previous step to make off-road dyed diesel more widely available had limited benefits for farm country over other options, according to two of the Trump officials and another administration official involved in the matter. Top agriculture lobbyists further warned the dyed diesel plan could actually backfire on farmers , because they could still be required to pay taxes on the product — just further down the road. So, Trump officials settled on the $8 billion tranche of direct money for farmers, given that similar kinds of payments to farmers — dating back during the president’s first trade war in 2018 — have quelled enough farmer and rural voter anger to shore up necessary support for Republicans during election season. Trump officials and Republican operatives in the Midwest are banking on the money shoring up support again this cycle — especially for GOP voters who are angry but also don’t want to vote for Democrats. Trump heads this Thursday to Iowa — where top Republicans have been worried about internal polling that warned several weeks ago they could lose all three Iowa House races, key Senate races and other once-safe red seats across farm states. "It's going to help bring farmers' votes out," Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told POLITICO of Trump’s plan on Tuesday. "This is some way that the federal government can step in to help farmers for problems that they face through no fault of their own,” he said. Most Hill Republicans weren’t given a heads-up about Trump’s announcement, including appropriators, and many hadn’t received any details from USDA as of Tuesday morning, according to two people familiar with the conversations who were granted anonymity to share private details. Top agriculture groups have warned they’d need at least $50 billion in direct aid this fall to make farmers whole following the impacts of tariffs, weather-related disasters and other high costs linked to the Iran war’s chokehold on agricultural supplies. Farm-state Republicans are pushing to add at least $12 billion in direct farm aid payments to a separate year-end legislative package. Monday’s aid rollout followed a number of other funding announcements made in swing rural districts. The White House doled out a first round of $12 billion in bailout funds earlier this year for growers of top agricultural commodities who were hit hard by Trump’s tariff agenda. Alongside Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins in Georgia, Rollins announced a $3.3 billion loan to build a power plant last week. Rollins rolled out $180 million in funding for seed research alongside vulnerable Iowa Reps. Zach Nunn and Marianette Miller-Meeks earlier this month. Trump also said he would approve long-derailed permanent year-round sales of ethanol during the Kansas rally — which would be a critical boon for corn growers across the Midwest. But the move has been long-stalled in Congress. “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it,” Trump said. “That’s a big deal for Kansas, actually.” Rachel Shin contributed reporting.
articles.headline: Trump just made a last-minute gambit to save farm-state Republicans in the midterms

articles.body: Americans are fed up with data centers and Big Tech, and Republicans are poised to take more of the political blame in the Nov. 3 midterms. The POLITICO Poll found last week that Americans were far more likely to associate the GOP with giving tax incentives to tech companies at a time when the public’s concerns about artificial intelligence and data center sprawl are only deepening. Nearly half of respondents — 47% — called Republicans the party of tech tax breaks, more than double the 21% who said the same for Democrats. Voters are also far more likely to want candidates who propose stripping away tax incentives for the data centers needed to fuel the AI boom, according to the new poll, conducted by PF Global. About a fifth of respondents said that ending those tax breaks would be among their most important tax issues in the midterms, while only 1 in 10 wanted to offer new preferences for data centers. The top tax priorities for voters, according to the poll, are hiking taxes on billionaires and curbing breaks for big companies. The findings come as lawmakers in both parties have scrambled to respond to the growing voter concerns over AI and data centers — and as Americans increasingly associate Silicon Valley titans with the Republican Party. But in both Democratic and Republican-led states alike, governors have sought to put new limits on tax incentives that were already approved for data centers. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) rolled out a proposal last week that would take that a step further by imposing a 100% tax on any state or local incentive offered to AI data centers. But it’s Democrats who have gone more on the offensive about the issue. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, for instance, has made data center incentives a key issue as he tries to unseat Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), a former state lawmaker and lieutenant governor. “Jon Husted’s ‘deals’ gave wealthy tech companies a windfall and left Ohioans footing the bill,” Brown recently posted on social media. Democrats have specifically homed in on Meta , which has cut its tax liability in recent years by billions of dollars as it builds out its AI products. And they have sought to tie expanded tax breaks approved by Republicans in last year’s megabill to the increase in data center construction. The GOP enacted incentives for companies in a broad array of industries as part of the 2025 tax cuts. But Big Tech has found those tax breaks particularly useful , helping to drive a big decrease in corporate tax payments as AI spending keeps trending upward. Meanwhile, Democrats with 2028 ambitions have floated new taxes on AI companies, while Democratic lawmakers have teed up legislation that would keep data centers from taking advantage of incentives like Opportunity Zones and bonus depreciation, both of which Republicans expanded in 2025. In fact, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) recently gave last year’s megabill another new name in a recent debate with his opponent, Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.). “I want to know if you will commit to voting to repeal that data center tax scam that you voted for,” Ossoff said. It’s not clear how much the current anti-AI energy will lead to new legislative limits in the coming months. But the new poll found Americans have a real fear of the unknown with artificial intelligence. A majority of respondents said that tech chief executives had been secretive about the potential risks of AI, while a plurality of Americans believe both that the risks of artificial intelligence development outweigh the benefits and that the government should strictly regulate the emerging technology.
articles.headline: Poll: Voters see Republicans as the party of Big Tech tax breaks

articles.body: ANCHORAGE — Alaska Republicans have railed for years against ranked-choice voting. Now some worry it could cost them in a critical Senate race. GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is facing not only well-known former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola in the four-way general-election field, but a same-name challenger who Republicans think could siphon votes from him in the close contest. Some GOP operatives fear the senator will lose first-choice votes to retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan Jr. — and that supporters of his longshot rival might not rank the incumbent at all in the state’s unusual election system where voters can pick backup options that get counted if no candidate clears 50% of the initial vote. Two recent polls that simulated ranked-choice tabulations showed Peltola as the victor. Art Hackney, a Sullivan ally who runs a super PAC boosting the senator, said Dan J. Sullivan is “going to get a percent of the vote” and warned it could “potentially” be "significant in terms of impacting" the result of the race. "Sullivan can win ... but it makes it a heck of a lot harder,” added a Republican operative working on other Alaska races. “It’s what the race is going to come down to: If he loses, it'll for sure be because of that. And if he wins, it'll be in spite of that." Republicans have for years bemoaned the system that allows voters to rank their preference and eliminates candidates until one reaches a majority as “costly” and “confusing,” and argue it has undercut their party . Top Republicans like outgoing GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy and President Donald Trump have urged voters to repeal the system via a ballot measure this fall after a previous effort failed two years ago . “Even if he gets a percent or 2% or 3% percent with the phony ranked choice stuff, you never know what they're going to do with it,” Trump said of Dan J. Sullivan in a rally in Wasilla last week, adding that it “could be the difference.” It’s happened before: Peltola benefited in her House win from a split GOP field, while Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) warded off a Trump-backed challenger in 2022 partly because of ranked-choice voting. Alaska Republicans are also fretting about the governor’s race this year, where three GOP candidates are competing, urging voters to “rank the red.” Dan J. Sullivan, Heikes and Peltola’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment. The similarly named Sullivans are separated on the ballot by their middle initials and party affiliation (the incumbent is listed as a Republican, the challenger without a party). But the senator and his allies aren’t taking any chances. They’re employing several of the tactics Murkowski used during her successful 2010 write-in campaign, including giving out rubber wristbands branded with the senator’s name and party affiliation, and airing a radio jingle with the NRSC . "Dan S. is your No. 1," the jingle goes. "If he’s not, rank him second, don’t throw your vote away. Dan S., Daniel, Gerry — just don’t rank Mary." "Dan S. Sullivan has two opponents in this race: Democrat Mary Peltola, and the ranked choice system she and her allies have deceptively manipulated to her advantage,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for the senator. “But our campaign is confident that Alaskans aren't confused. They know the real Dan, and we're making sure every voter can find him: ballot facsimiles on every mailer, voters reached at the door and on the phone, and even a jingle.” Those pushing to keep ranked-choice voting in Alaska argue the system helps mitigate the so-called spoiler effect. The group behind this year's repeal measure said in an email that it's a nonpartisan effort focused solely on eliminating the system. Outside GOP groups boosting Sullivan like Americans for Prosperity Action and Club for Growth Action have been urging voters at doors and via mailers to rank the incumbent first, a slightly different approach than Sullivan’s campaign. “Make Republican Incumbent DAN S. SULLIVAN your 1ST CHOICE and ONLY CHOICE,” read one Club for Growth Action mailer seen by POLITICO. “In a tight election, it doesn't take a ton of people to get confused to possibly change the trajectory and the outcome,” said Kevin Greene, senior adviser for AFP Action in Alaska. A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro .

articles.body: CHICAGO — JB Pritzker is pouring tens of millions of dollars of his own money into boosting Black and Hispanic candidates this cycle. That could help him win over critical voters in 2028. The billionaire Illinois governor — who’s also considered a potential presidential contender — is investing at least $38 million in battleground races, according to a person familiar with the governor’s political strategy granted anonymity to discuss details. Much of that spending has gone to candidates of color, some of whom haven’t drawn much other investment from national Democrats. Pritzker is also investing in races in all six early states on the Democratic presidential nominating calendar, which was rearranged earlier this year to give prize spots to five states with significant Black or Hispanic communities: South Carolina, Nevada, New Mexico, Virginia and Michigan. Asked by POLITICO about how his midterms spending could lay the groundwork for a presidential campaign, Pritzker said he’s “focused on winning in 2026.” But some of those receiving major infusions from Pritzker say it should earn him a serious look in 2028. “Governor Pritzker is playing a very important role” in the party, said Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat facing an uphill fight in Alabama who has gotten an assist from Pritzker’s newly formed super PAC, Ready for the Fight. “He actually cares and is … willing to invest in districts where minority candidates have a good shot if they have the right type of support. I think that's an important element of any leadership.” Pritzker said Ready for the Fight’s strategy focuses on GOP-leaning districts that would normally be “out of sight for Democrats” but have become competitive in a favorable midterm environment.   Figures is fighting for reelection in a district Republicans redrew to make it harder for a Democrat to win by decreasing the Black population, after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act this past spring . When that court decision came down, Figures said Pritzker was one of the first people to call him to offer help. “The fact that he reached out and engaged us through that lens with that level of knowledge about what was happening in Alabama meant a lot to us,” Figures said. Pritzker is spending $1.6 million for Figures, $1.9 million to boost Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, another Black candidate running in a newly gerrymandered district that includes part of Memphis, and has put $1.3 million behind Arkansas Democrat Chris Jones in his race against Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) in Little Rock, making him the largest Democratic spender besides the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in all three districts. Pritzker is also the largest individual donor to Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial campaign, personally contributing $200,000 before committing another $1 million earlier this month. The latter donation came around the same time the Democratic Governors Association also contributed $1 million. Hispanic officials and lawmakers have been ramping up the pressure on the group’s chair, fellow 2028 hopeful Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest more in Texas. Pritzker called Hinojosa an “outstanding person.” “The opportunity for her to win and for Democrats to win as a result of her winning is tremendous,” Pritzker told POLITICO at a Thursday press conference. “From my perspective, we all ought to be helping somebody like that to overcome the odds.” And while he declined to criticize national Democrats’ strategic decisions not to spend for some candidates in tough races facing a deluge of GOP outside money, he made clear he was looking to make up for that lack of funding. “If I were running in one of those districts, and I’m not getting dollars that I see going to other districts, I would feel frustrated,” Pritzker said. “There's only so much you can do when you're being outspent 3 to 1 or 4 to 1 nationally, and so I'm trying to do my best to fill in some of that wherever I can.” Pritzker is not the only potential 2028er looking to woo politically powerful Black and Hispanic communities, and his day job and his own reelection bid keeps him away from the national trail — unlike some of the other senators and governors who’ve been crisscrossing the country for months. But what he lacks in time, he makes up for in money. His spending strategy is catching the attention of senior Black Democratic leaders. “People tend to take notice of the people who take notice of them,” said South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Clyburn said he takes Pritzker “seriously” as a potential presidential candidate but cautioned that Black voters and organizers in his home state, where Pritzker recently addressed the state NAACP’s annual convention, likely won’t be swayed by campaign contributions alone. “We are going to take measure of candidates, not based upon how deep their pockets are, but we're going to take measure of how deep their commitments are to those things deemed important in the African American community,” he said. Still, the donations are helping the billionaire longtime Democratic donor and two-term governor forge new allies in key communities that could provide a boost come primary season. “I appreciate Governor Pritzker’s willingness to invest in places others have written off,” said Jones, who also thanked the DCCC for recently adding him to their list of targeted races. “Convincing people a race is worth investing in has often been an insurmountable barrier for Black candidates.” Pritzker’s PAC spent $2.8 million for New Mexico Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez, and the governor made a $400,000 personal contribution into a super PAC backing Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, a Black candidate running in a heavily Hispanic early-voting state. But his biggest investment of the cycle was to boost Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who he picked as his 2018 running mate when she was a little-known state representative, then invested $10 million to help her win her U.S. Senate primary this spring. The move created some tensions: Pritzker’s endorsement of Stratton helped lift her 2026 Senate campaign significantly over two other candidates — including Rep. Robin Kelly (D-Ill.), another Black woman who has had a strained relationship with Pritzker over the years. That frustrated several members of the Congressional Black Caucus, though he’s sought to mend fences since. Clyburn, who endorsed and campaigned for Kelly, said that race won’t “dictate future relationships when it comes to putting our party in the best position to win the elections in 2028.” And ultimately, Stratton’s ascendance is a significant step in Pritzker's outreach to Black voters nationally. He will be credited with helping send just the sixth Black woman ever to the U.S. Senate after her likely victory in November. She could be a key 2028 surrogate should he run for president. “He really does have a platform to raise awareness of critical races that people might not otherwise pay attention to,” Stratton said. “I'm really grateful for that.” CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misstated the nature of DGA's donations to the Texas governor's race; it was made independently from Pritzker's.
articles.headline: JB Pritzker’s midterm strategy wins the attention of Black and Hispanic Democrats

articles.body: Democrats are salivating over, and Republicans are bracing for, a potentially massive blue wave. One GOP pollster is urging everyone to calm down. Patrick Ruffini, a founding partner at Echelon Insights, has been loudly throwing cold water on Democrats’ hopes of sweeping the red state Senate seats that have become battlegrounds in a worsening national environment for Republicans. “The polls are, I think, intentionally inflating the size of the battleground,” Ruffini told POLITICO. Democrats are pushing to flip Senate seats in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — all states that President Donald Trump won by at least 11 points in 2024 — with dreams of going even deeper into the map Kansas, South Carolina and even Mississippi. Sensing a potential disaster, Republicans have significantly curtailed their investments in North Carolina and Georgia to direct resources elsewhere. Ruffini, who isn’t polling for candidates or party committees in any federal races, said he’s skeptical of Democrats flipping some of those seats, particularly in the Midwest, and gives the GOP a coin flip’s chance at keeping control of the Senate. If a blue wave were to come, he said it would defy the ingrained partisanship in deep-red states that has mirrored growing political polarization around the country. “I think it would be somewhat of a historic shift if that were to happen,” he said. Here’s more from POLITICO’s chat with Ruffini, edited for length and clarity. A more condensed version of this interview ran in POLITICO’s Morning Score campaign newsletter. You've been pretty publicly skeptical of polling that indicates a big tsunami for Democrats in November. Why is that? I think we can read the environment right, but the map wrong. The pretty large shift towards Democrats that we're seeing on the generic ballot and in a lot of individual races, I'm not saying that's not going to materialize. What I am more skeptical of is… the ability of any major party in this polarized era that we're in to rack up significant gains in states that went double digits for the other side. I’m not ruling out — I think there will be some [examples]. I think Alaska is one where it's both an idiosyncratic state, and [Democratic nominee Mary] Peltola has shown some specific candidate-centered strength. Nor would it shock me if [Democrat] James Talarico wins, despite the history in Texas. That would not surprise me, just given the candidate quality disparity, particularly on the Ken Paxton side. Where I get more skeptical is when you move into the Midwest, where there has historically been pretty large polling errors [overstating Democrats’ chances] in states like Iowa, Ohio. And I think you can extend that to the Democratic enthusiasm around Kansas. Is your skepticism coming more from the quality of the individual polls that you’re seeing that are showing massive Democratic surges in the Midwest, or is it the history of these states that you’re betting will ultimately win out? I think fundamentals are going to play an important role, particularly in states where there was a solid Trump advantage. We're not talking about a state like North Carolina or Georgia that’s only for Trump narrowly, where Democrats, at least in the Senate races, are clearly favored. Historically the presumption is that states tend to converge on their base partisanship in the closing days of an election, but especially that's been the pattern in the Midwest. Specifically as it relates to the polls this year, I think any pollster you would talk to, including myself, is experiencing significant non-response bias favoring Democrats. When you're seeing high-propensity Democrats [responding to polls] at twice the rate of high-propensity Republicans, when we know that the turnout on both sides would be roughly evenly paired, that's a warning sign for polling in this cycle. It seems like there’s some GOP internal polling saying that Republicans are worried about these states, because they are moving money around to triage certain races . I’m curious if you feel like they’re wrong to be making those decisions? Absolutely not. They're not wrong. You do have to take the polls somewhat seriously in the sense of, if you do get a poll that's within the margin of error, I think you're duty-bound to spend money in those places and not to ignore what could be a potential signal. I think that control of the Senate comes down to Texas, so they're right to be spending money there. If you just look at the amount of money being spent in Texas versus Kansas, obviously it's a much, much bigger state, and you need to spend much more money. But it's not something along the lines of ‘the battleground has shifted. It's a foregone conclusion. Democrats are going to win the Senate,’ and then the battleground entirely shifts to a state like Kansas or to Iowa, right? I don't think we're seeing that. It sounds like the issue you have is how the broader public is interpreting these polls rather than the polls themselves? The polls are, I think, intentionally inflating the size of the battleground. And to some extent it's happening both ways. The polls showing a margin-of- error race in Minnesota is possible, right? I'm not as concerned about a polling error in Minnesota as I am in Kansas. But because of the number of Democratic internals and because of the incentive of Democratic internals to show close races across the battleground, what you generally tend to see is more of an inflated sense of how big the battleground actually is. A lot of these races just break a certain way. We've reported that Republicans are privately conceding that the House is lost. Is that your reading of the data too? That's the best reading of the data. That said, if there's a three-point polling error or something, then I think it gets very, very tight and anything can happen. But I think that's the most likely outcome. What is your prediction for the number of Senate seats Republicans will have? My prediction for both the probability and the seat count is 50-50. There's a 50-50 chance Republicans hold the Senate. I think if they do, it's with 50 seats, probably. But obviously, that can tilt very easily. Which of these states do you think are going to flip for Democrats? Alaska is clearly favored. I mean, I don't know if it's clearly favored, but I think it's at least still Democrat. I think Texas is going to be very, very close. I just think the partisanship of the state is — people forget it's a little bit more Republican than it was back in 2018. I think Republicans are probably being underestimated in Ohio because of the past Midwestern polling error. At the same time, I would say it's still uphill in Maine and Michigan to some degree. I think Susan Collins has really been the lone bright spot, at least in terms of the conventional wisdom, the narrative in the Senate for Republicans. I think she has a fighting chance, but I think Republicans are still probably under a 50% chance in both Michigan and Maine, just due to the nature of their partisan lean. If at the end of all of this it is a real blue wave in the Senate, what will have happened to have made you wrong? If that happens, we will have seen a level of depolarization in the electorate that we haven't seen since around 2012. You really have to go back in history for a state like Kansas to flip.That would be pretty unique historically, where it's a flip where you have an incumbent losing. That's the kind of thing that used to happen in Senate races a lot, and then things, starting with Trump, got a lot more polarized. So what that would mean is, maybe this is the start of a new political era. But I think it would be somewhat of a historic shift if that were to happen.

articles.body: <p>Una mayoría de los doce magistrados que componen el Tribunal Constitucional defenderá este miércoles que se inadmita el recurso de amparo presentado por el Defensor del Pueblo, según fuentes del órgano de garantías. El recurso pedía restablecer el derecho al voto de más de 160.000 españoles, nacionalizados en virtud de la <i>ley de nietos</i>, que viven en el extranjero y a quien el Tribunal Supremo ha retirado cautelarmente el sufragio a poco más de un mes de las próximas elecciones generales. La mayoría del Pleno, sin reflejar esta vez la división de referencia entre progresistas y conservadores, considera que como el Supremo abrió un plazo de alegaciones para los afectados —vigente hasta el viernes, 23 de octubre—, el recurso del Defensor es prematuro y no cumple con el requisito de subsidiariedad del amparo: esto es, que se haya agotado la vía de la justicia ordinaria. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-21/el-constitucional-se-dispone-a-rechazar-el-amparo-presentado-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/V2MXRRXOOZGIZOKEIPR5NB3D5Q.JPG?auth=0bcb411e82f4b1d558bd28a8b3bef923298f349e4dfa63a28828be559beeb8eb" width="8192" height="5464" alt="Vecinos y voluntarios limpian el barro en una calle junto al río Girona en Els Poblets."></img><p>La impresión del desastre es la misma que <a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/gota-fria/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/gota-fria/">dos años atrás</a>: el barro que lo cubre todo, las puertas desvencijadas, los muebles amontonados en la calle, las excavadoras y los camiones cargados de residuos y mucha gente con cepillos, fregonas, escobones, cubos o mangueras. La imagen del pequeño municipio alicantino de Els Poblets apenas se distingue de la de cualquiera de los pueblos que fueron pasto de la dana del 29 de octubre de 2024, que se cobró <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/la-leccion-aprendida-de-la-dana-de-2024-las-alertas-masivas-y-la-prevencion-son-clave-para-salvar-vidas.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/la-leccion-aprendida-de-la-dana-de-2024-las-alertas-masivas-y-la-prevencion-son-clave-para-salvar-vidas.html">la vida de 233 personas </a>en la provincia de Valencia. La sensación de <i>déjà vu </i>es inevitable, pero con una diferencia insoslayable: la magnitud de la tragedia.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/comunidad-valenciana/2026-10-21/voluntarios-de-la-dana-de-2024-que-ahora-limpian-su-pueblo-inundado-el-barro-es-el-mismo-pero-el-desastre-es-menor.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/GE7A6A2O25EF5IMFBOGRTX57KA.JPG?auth=b526dd270747116f4d9dda121f960cbc76ac306490f8bcdb6ec37ed4f17ef4f4" width="8102" height="5404" alt="Una joven arroja residuos en la limpieza de Els Poblets, este martes."></img><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/QDATEMP5C5GFJKDEUSUDMQUGDQ.JPG?auth=3b1c9df97d5d8b8017c254e32c094b91de7338edf6896e246636af3517c49a7d" width="8107" height="5407" alt="Un joven, desatascando una alcantariila en Els Poblets."></img><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/Q6FXPUJXHRA63GUNJTVI4TWCPA.JPG?auth=32109d95ce46c0b7732ca9159ac892bf6a4c7027a03610404eaf426b3c90b550" width="4016" height="2678" alt="Un hombre descansa sobre un carro repleto de aparatos y cajas de herramientas en la tarde del martes en Els Poblets."></img>

articles.body: <p>Los militares desplegados en Ceuta están en el ojo del huracán. El Hospital Universitario de la ciudad autónoma ha remitido al juzgado de guardia una veintena de <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-19/el-hospital-de-ceuta-remite-al-juez-una-veintena-de-partes-de-lesiones-de-inmigrantes-que-dicen-haber-sido-agredidos-por-militares.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-19/el-hospital-de-ceuta-remite-al-juez-una-veintena-de-partes-de-lesiones-de-inmigrantes-que-dicen-haber-sido-agredidos-por-militares.html">partes de lesiones de inmigrantes</a> que dicen haber sido golpeados por miembros de las Fuerzas Armadas. Pero los indocumentados no son los únicos que resultan heridos en estos enfrentamientos que se vienen repitiendo tras la irrupción <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/choque-entre-el-gobierno-de-ceuta-y-la-moncloa-por-la-devolucion-de-migrantes-pendiente.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/choque-entre-el-gobierno-de-ceuta-y-la-moncloa-por-la-devolucion-de-migrantes-pendiente.html">de más de 70.000 inmigrantes</a> a través del paso del Tarajal los pasados 30 y 31 de julio. Al menos 11 soldados han resultado heridos de diversa consideración desde que el Ejército se desplegó en misión de disuasión, vigilancia y apoyo a las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado, según fuentes de Defensa. El último, el pasado fin de semana, cuando uno de ellos se fracturó un dedo. Varios han sido trasladados al hospital Gómez Ulla de Madrid para someterse a intervenciones quirúrgicas. La mayoría de las lesiones, según las mismas fuentes, se ha producido en el curso de forcejeos y persecuciones, pero también ha habido apedreamientos. El más grave, a finales de agosto en la zona de Benzú, cuando <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-06/identificados-21-migrantes-por-lanzar-piedras-contra-una-patrulla-militar-y-guardias-civiles-en-ceuta.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-06/identificados-21-migrantes-por-lanzar-piedras-contra-una-patrulla-militar-y-guardias-civiles-en-ceuta.html">decenas de inmigrantes lanzaron piedras a una patrulla</a>, con un saldo de cuatro soldados heridos y una docena de marroquíes detenidos.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-21/al-menos-11-militares-han-resultado-heridos-en-enfrentamientos-con-inmigrantes-en-ceuta.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/3TLZHPSBF5CM5OR2SD5DBVE47Q.jpg?auth=43f34b26aea2346a3149bca7ec74758eb14246903a2c6c9f045e3e94014ddd9d" width="4724" height="3150" alt="Militares vigilando una barriada en Ceuta."></img><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/T4RZWRTKLRFOVO4BQL3TJ3KQOU.jpg?auth=6849aa031b43d033e985cae1bf771f65364718e7917a1ea8b0509a41f800e567" width="2000" height="1326" alt="Un joven inmigrante muestra en Ceuta la cura de las lesiones supuestamente causadas por militares y el parte médico del pasado 4 de octubre."></img>

articles.body: <p>El Tribunal Supremo ha aplicado este martes la amnistía al exvicepresidente de la Generalitat Oriol Junqueras y a los exconsejeros Raül Romeva, Dolors Bassa y Jordi Turull. Dos semanas después de que <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-06/via-libre-al-regreso-de-puigdemont-el-constitucional-ordena-al-supremo-que-amnistie-la-malversacion-del-proces.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-06/via-libre-al-regreso-de-puigdemont-el-constitucional-ordena-al-supremo-que-amnistie-la-malversacion-del-proces.html">el Tribunal Constitucional estableciera que la Sala Penal debió otorgar la medida de gracia al delito de malversación</a> que atribuyó a los exdirigentes independentistas, el Supremo ha cumplido este mandato y ha amnistiado a los cuatro antiguos miembros del Govern a los que juzgó y condenó por ese delito en 2019. La amnistía deja sin efecto la pena de inhabilitación que aún pesaba sobre ellos, por lo que los cuatro podrían ya presentarse a las próximas elecciones u ocupar un cargo público. En el auto en el que expone su decisión, el Supremo lanza al Constitucional un reproche insólito, por extenso y contundente. “Su innecesaria grandilocuencia revela el deseo de adornar un razonamiento invasivo del ámbito jurisdiccional que corresponde al Tribunal Supremo”, recalcan los jueces. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/el-supremo-asume-la-doctrina-del-constitucional-y-amnistia-a-junqueras-y-tres-exconsejeros.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El Partido Popular y Vox aproximan posiciones para concurrir con más fuerza al Senado en las elecciones del 29 de noviembre. Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha confirmado este martes que ambas formaciones negocian en estos momentos para <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-18/un-frente-de-izquierdas-y-otro-de-derechas-se-disputaran-a-cara-de-perro-el-control-del-senado.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-18/un-frente-de-izquierdas-y-otro-de-derechas-se-disputaran-a-cara-de-perro-el-control-del-senado.html">encontrar una fórmula que les permita lograr una mayoría más holgada</a> frente a la papeleta conjunta de PSOE y Frente Amplio. Una vez cerrado el plazo para presentar coaliciones, el viernes pasado, PP y ultras barajan otros planes. En una entrevista en Cope, Feijóo ha apuntado como escenario más plausible el de que los ultras no se presenten en determinadas circunscripciones y que el Partido Popular ceda senadores por designación autonómica como contrapartida. El líder del PP quiere un pacto, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-17/vox-baraja-no-presentarse-al-senado-en-algunas-provincias-para-evitar-una-mayoria-de-izquierdas.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-17/vox-baraja-no-presentarse-al-senado-en-algunas-provincias-para-evitar-una-mayoria-de-izquierdas.html">mete presión a Santiago Abascal</a> y busca con ese planteamiento controlar los tres quintos de la Cámara alta, lo que le permitiría hacer nombramientos sin tener que pactar con el PSOE. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-20/feijoo-confirma-negociaciones-con-vox-para-las-listas-del-senado-si-estan-a-la-altura-el-pp-tambien.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Poco después de que la Aemet lanzara el pasado viernes el primer aviso sobre la llegada de una dana<a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/temporales/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/temporales/"> a la que bautizó como <i>Adam</i></a>, la Generalitat Valenciana publicó un <i>post </i>en las redes para recordar a la población qué pasos tenía que seguir en caso de que en los siguientes días recibieran un ES-Alert en sus móviles: “Deja el coche en zonas seguras. No atravieses calles llenas de agua. Evita desplazamientos. Infórmate siempre por canales oficiales”. Eran las 14.27 del 16 de octubre y los primeros efectos del temporal en la región valenciana no llegarían hasta dos días después. En esas 48 horas, el Gobierno autonómico actualizó constantemente en sus redes el temporal e incluso envió un mensaje masivo a los teléfonos para anunciar con un día de antelación el riesgo de inundaciones en el litoral norte e interior sur de Valencia. El resto de publicaciones y Es-Alert han sido precisos, insistiendo a la población en que se subiera a plantas altas en zonas inundables. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/la-leccion-aprendida-de-la-dana-de-2024-las-alertas-masivas-y-la-prevencion-son-clave-para-salvar-vidas.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/5JX72G7KUBHBHIWJ6COQWH5UNY.jpg?auth=49d026f1ba49d9c04b03c88c5ca6e147a7f65dd06b2dabdd0d73588c0fd26537" width="6720" height="4480" alt="Vista de una calle de Els Poblets, Alicante, tras las inundaciones provocada por la dana 'Adam' este lunes."></img><h3>En directo | Última hora del temporal en España, en directo | Se levanta el confinamiento en los ocho municipios de la Comunidad Valenciana| </h3><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/5JX72G7KUBHBHIWJ6COQWH5UNY.jpg?auth=49d026f1ba49d9c04b03c88c5ca6e147a7f65dd06b2dabdd0d73588c0fd26537" width="6720" height="4480" alt="Vista de una calle de Els Poblets, Alicante, tras las inundaciones provocada por la dana 'Adam', este lunes"></img>

articles.body: <p>La Unidad Central Operativa (UCO) de la Guardia Civil cuestiona que uno de los vehículos del comisionista Víctor de Aldama sufriese un tiroteo como amenaza, según consta en uno de sus informes enviados a la Audiencia Nacional. Los agentes han interceptado varias comunicaciones donde el empresario informa a la aseguradora de que le “han intentado robar” en su Audi A8 y que han tratado de “romper el cristal” con un “punzón”, pero no lo “han conseguido”. “No hemos puesto denuncia porque no lo hemos visto. Ha sido de madrugada y poner denuncia es ridículo porque es perder tres horas”, añadió Víctor de Aldama.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/la-uco-cuestiona-la-veracidad-del-tiroteo-al-coche-de-aldama.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>La Junta Electoral Central (JEC) <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-15/la-jec-ordena-a-la-oficina-del-censo-electoral-que-remita-a-los-27-millones-inscritos-en-el-exterior-la-documentacion-para-poder-votar.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-15/la-jec-ordena-a-la-oficina-del-censo-electoral-que-remita-a-los-27-millones-inscritos-en-el-exterior-la-documentacion-para-poder-votar.html">acordó la semana pasada que se empezara a enviar</a> a los inscritos en el censo del extranjero la documentación necesaria para poder participar en las elecciones generales el 29 de noviembre, pero incluyendo en ese envío una advertencia con la posibilidad de que el derecho al voto haya quedado afectado por <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-12/el-supremo-mantiene-para-el-29-n-la-suspension-del-derecho-al-voto-de-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-12/el-supremo-mantiene-para-el-29-n-la-suspension-del-derecho-al-voto-de-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html">la decisión del Tribunal Supremo respecto a la ley de nietos</a>. La JEC envió a la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administativo el texto pactado y los jueces han dado este martes 24 horas a las partes para que presenten alegaciones sobre el contenido de ese escrito. El partido Iustitia Europa, el primero en llevar al alto tribunal los efectos electorales de la Ley de Memoria Democrática, ya ha registrado su respuesta, en la que reclama que se advierta a las autoridades y funcionarios responsables de que incumplir los autos del Supremo podría constituir un delito electoral. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-20/el-supremo-pregunta-a-las-partes-por-el-acuerdo-de-la-junta-electoral-sobre-el-voto-exterior.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El juez de la Audiencia Nacional Antonio Piña ha enviado a prisión, acusados de delitos de terrorismo, a los dos disidentes de la izquierda <i>abertzale </i>detenidos por la Ertzaintza el sábado después de que se <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-17/la-ertzaintza-detiene-en-irun-a-dos-personas-acusadas-de-terrorismo-y-con-informacion-sobre-las-fuerzas-de-seguridad.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-17/la-ertzaintza-detiene-en-irun-a-dos-personas-acusadas-de-terrorismo-y-con-informacion-sobre-las-fuerzas-de-seguridad.html">presentaran en la comisaría de Irún</a> acompañados de su abogado. Se trata de Aratz Bilbao Gómez, de 34 años, y Malen Grünig Ibáñez, de 23 años, a los que el magistrado considera integrantes de Jardun Koordinadora, una organización integrada por <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2021-10-20/los-ultimos-restos-de-eta.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2021-10-20/los-ultimos-restos-de-eta.html">disidentes de la izquierda abertzale</a> supuestamente contrarios a <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-18/los-ultimos-pasos-del-final-del-terrorismo-etarra.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-18/los-ultimos-pasos-del-final-del-terrorismo-etarra.html">la decisión que tomó ETA en octubre de 2011 de abandonar la violencia</a>. Bilbao es señalado como “el motor principal” de este colectivo e “impulsor y dinamizador” del mismo. A su compañera, el magistrado la describe como “militante activa”. El magistrado esgrime para ordenar su encarcelamiento tanto riesgo de fuga como de reiteración delictiva de ambos, que tenían antecedentes policiales por “actos violentos” en otros países europeos.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/el-juez-envia-a-prision-por-terrorismo-a-los-dos-disidentes-de-la-izquierda-abertzale-detenidos-por-la-ertzaintza.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: Els veïns del carrer d’Olzinelles , propers a la plaça de Bonet i Moixí, van ser testimonis divendres passat d’una escena digna de pel·lícula d’acció . Diversos testimonis han explicat a l’ Infobarris que un home va provocar moments de tensió aquella nit. Encara amb l’ensurt al cos, recorden que l’ individu va caure al pati d’un restaurant i va irrompre dins l’habitatge d’una veïna, la Sandra. Després d’accedir a diversos patis i provocar diverses destrosses, l’home va ser interceptat al carrer de Finlàndia i dut a l’ hospital . A hores d’ara, el Mossos d’Esquadra investiguem l’individu per un presumpte delicte de violació de domicili jurídic , sense voluntat d’ocupació. Els veïns van sentir un fort estrèpit Segons relata la Sandra els fets van començar minuts abans de les onze de la nit. Ella i les seves dues filles estaven al llit xerrant, quan van sentir un estrèpit al pati interior de la finca . “Vam pensar que havia caigut alguna cosa grossa, un aparell d’aire condicionat, i molts veïns vam treure el cap per veure què passava”, explica. Els treballadors del restaurant japonès van veure com un home havia caigut al pati de l’establiment, després de trencar una coberta de fibra de vidre . Expliquen que l’impacte fins i tot va abonyegar un dels electrodomèstics . Poc després de caure l’home va saltar i va accedir al pati dels baixos , on viu la Sandra. Tot que la veïna va reaccionar ràpid per tancar el pestell de les portes d’accés, l’home va aconseguir entrar dins l’habitatge aprofitant una finestra corredissa que no estava tancada del tot . “Era molt àgil, va trencar bona part de l’estenedor en entrar”, recorda la veïna. Va irrompre a casa d’una veïna Un cop a l’interior del pis, l’home va causar destrosses importants . “Va arrasar amb tot. Va tirar els mobles, electrodomèstics, la roba, els estris… amb la intenció d’atrinxerar-se i dificultar el pas”, explica la Sandra. En aquell moment la Sandra va donar instruccions a les dues menors perquè es refugiessin en una de les habitacions amb pestell. “Vaig començar a cridar fort per demanar ajuda”, explica. Aleshores va intentar convèncer l’home perquè abandonés el pis. “Jo li deia que tenia dues nenes a casa i que havia de marxar. Obria la port perquè sortís, però ell me la tornava a tancar mentre repetia que no volia sortir”, recorda. Tot i l’estat de nerviosisme que mostrava, la Sandra assegura que en cap moment va intentar agredir-les . “Estava molt espantat. No sé d’on venia ni perquè corria, però no venia a fer-nos mal”, afirma. Els Mossos d’Esquadra han explicat que l’individu no era perseguit per cap agent i, a hores d’ara, desconeixen els motius del seu comportament. Finalment, després d’uns minuts de tensió , l’home va tornar a fugir pels patins interiors, fins que va arribar al carrer de Finlàndia , on va ser atès per personal sanitari, segons han confirmat a l’ Infobarris els Serveis d’Emergències Mèdiques (SEM). articles.body: L’ Ajuntament de Barcelona ha ofert a la Sareb (Societat de Gestió d’Actius Procedents de la Reestructuració Bancària) entre 3,5 i 4 milions d’euros per comprar el solar on hi ha l’ Àgora Juan Andrés Benítez , al Raval. El tinent d’alcaldia d’Urbanisme, Jordi Valls, així ho ha explicat durant la Comissió d’Ecologia, Urbanisme, Mobilitat i Habitatge d’aquest dimarts, 20 d’octubre. Valls ha explicat que “encara l’ operació no està tancada però sí que hi ha una oferta formal “. Cal recordar que sota aquest solar, ubicat al carrer de l’Aurora, número 13, hi havia una ordre de desallotjament prevista per al 15 d’octubre però que es va suspendre després que l’Ajuntament fes l’oferta als propietaris del solar. Pendent de la resposta de la Sareb Valls ha revelat que l’Ajuntament està en espera de saber la resposta de la Sareb a l’oferta municipal i també de quin serà el preu final de l’operació. Així mateix, el tinent d’alcaldia d’Urbanisme ha explicat que “l’ ús de l’espai es decidirà més endavant si bé el que se sap és que aquest solar té capacitat per a 20 o 25 habitatges “. Les diferents entitats que fan ús de l’espai sempre han defensat que els agradaria que el solar continués tenint un ús comunitari però que el que consideraven més important és que fos un ús públic. 12 anys de lluita veïnal L ‘ espai està ocupat des del 5 d’octubre del 2014 . La data no va ser aleatòria. Es complia el primer aniversari de l’homicidi imprudent del veí i activista del barri Juan Andrés Benítez a mans de vuit mossos d’esquadra. Des de llavors l’espai el gestionen un grup d’entitats del Raval que asseguren que han convertit el solar en un punt de cohesió i referència al barri. El desallotjament del 15 d’octubre era el quart intent de la propietat de recuperar el solar. articles.body: L’oposició ha reprovat la tinenta d’alcaldia d’Urbanisme, Laia Bonet , per les rehabilitacions de pisos del barri del Besòs i el Maresme . Segons denuncien els veïns són defectuoses . El suspens polític a Bonet s’ha produït a la Comissió d’Ecologia, Urbanisme, Mobilitat i Habitatge d’aquest dimarts a la tarda i ha estat a proposta de BComú amb el suport de Junts , el PP i Vox , l’abstenció d’ ERC i els vot en contra del govern del PSC . BComú ha impulsat la iniciativa perquè els veïns que viuen en finques que ja s’han rehabilitat denuncien defectes en les obres executades , com ara acabats poc polits, rajoles trencades, goteres, finestres que no tanquen i avaries en ascensors i intèrfons. Es tracta dels veïns dels 10 primers blocs (d’uns 200 que s’han de rehabilitar per problemes estructurals) on s’hi va començar a actuar fa cinc anys en el marc d’una prova pilot. Tret d’un bloc on els treballs van acabar fa tres anys, a la resta les actuacions encara estan en marxa. Un òrgan que ha de servir per fer “ un salt d’escala “, ha dit Bonet, en la regeneració de pisos del barri. Gràcies a la creació d’aquesta empresa mixta, en els pròxims anys s’injectaran 415 milions d’euros al Besòs i al Maresme per rehabilitar tot el parc d’habitatges que, ara com ara, té problemes estructurals greus i pisos amb estances apuntalades . Per Bonet l’acord és “important” perquè el model actual d’actuació ha quedat demostrat que és “limitat”. “Se n’han rehabilitat 192 habitatges en quatre anys, hem d’esperar 40 anys més per rehabilitar el barri?”, ha dit. articles.body: (ACN/Redacció) Tret de sortida a la 38a edició del 080 Barcelona Fashion . El certamen ha arrencat amb la desfilada de moda circular 080 Reborn , una proposta centrada en roba de segona mà i en la reutilització dels tèxtils per allargar la vida útil de les peces. Des d’aquest dimarts i fins dijous, desfilaran a la passarel·la del Port Vell les col·leccions de 26 marques i dissenyadors , amb noms com Custo Barcelona , Dominnico, Guillermina Baeza , Surkana, David Catalan i Aleixandri Studio. També et pot interessar Un 080 Barcelona Fashion per reivindicar-se internacionalment amb 26 desfilades Àlex Jassé Redacció 1 minut de lectura Creadors emergents i consolidats A més dels dissenyadors consolidats, la programació inclou propostes de creadors emergents i activitats paral·leles vinculades a la moda i la seva dimensió cultural. Una n’és la iniciativa PLEC-Barcelona Cultura de Moda , impulsada per l’Ajuntament de Barcelona amb l’objectiu d’apropar la moda a la ciutadania i reforçar-ne la dimensió cultural. Com a l’edició de primavera, les desfilades es fan a la passarel·la de grans dimensions ubicada a l’entorn portuari de l’espai Marina Vela . Foto: Andrea Salazar (ACN) El pes econòmic de la moda Durant la inauguració, el conseller d’Empresa i Treball, Miquel Sàmper , ha valorat el pes econòmic del sector a Catalunya. Sàmper ha explicat que la moda i el tèxtil mouen 17.500 milions d’euros i donen feina directa a 74.000 treballadors de tot el territori. El conseller també ha defensat que es tracta d’un sector que cal reforçar i ha remarcat la necessitat de captar talent de les noves generacions. articles.body: (ACN/Redacció) Educació no retirarà les pissarres digitals de les aules d’I3, I4 i I5 , com va anunciar que faria el juny del 2025 , però en suprimirà els “usos lliures” i no tindran connexió a internet . Així es desprèn de l’actualització del Pla de digitalització responsable que ha publicat la conselleria i que planteja un model d ‘ús “pedagògic, restringit i segur” . Ho ha avançat El Periódico i ho han confirmat fonts d’Educació a l’ACN. Tot plegat coincideix amb la petició d’accelerar les mesures per reduir les pantalles als centres educatius . També et pot interessar Illa es referma en la limitació de l’accés a la IA i aposta per recuperar els llibres a les aules Andrea Muñoz 2 minuts de lectura Ús pedagògic, restringit i segur de les pissarres El document, titulat Les pissarres educatives a l’educació infantil , planteja un model d’ús “pedagògic, restringit i segur” d’aquests recursos. “La pissarra digital no ha de ser una pantalla d’ús permanent. S’ha d’utilitzar quan aporti valor a l’activitat educativa compartida (afavorir la conversa, el llenguatge oral, l’observació conjunta, la creativitat, l’escolta, els projectes col·laboratius i la construcció compartida del coneixement)”, indica el text. Alhora, remarca que se n’ha de controlar el temps d’ús i insisteix que “ la tecnologia no substitueix l’experiència educativa ”, sinó que és el docent qui, seguint el seu criteri pedagògic, ha de decidir quan utilitzar-la de manera limitada i intencionada per enriquir la pràctica a l’aula. També et pot interessar L’ús de pantalles, un problema de salut pública que pot provocar “danys irreversibles” Sandra García Prat 1 minut de lectura Tres nivells d’accés i un perfil infantil La conselleria crearà un perfil específic d’usuari, anomenat infantil , amb funcionalitats limitades i un entorn simplificat, que evitarà les distraccions i la sobreestimulació visual dels alumnes d’I3, I4 i I5. A més, establirà tres nivells d’accés : el del docent, protegit amb contrasenya i amb accés a totes les funcionalitats multimèdia; el de l’administrador, amb accés complet per gestionar la pissarra, i el de classe, amb accés directe, però amb les limitacions esmentades. Així, amb el perfil infantil no es podrà navegar lliurement per internet i només es podrà accedir a recursos autoritzats. Tot plegat coincideix amb la petició d’accelerar les mesures per reduir l’ús de pantalles als centres educatius que Aixeca el cap ha fet aquest dimarts davant la Comissió d’Educació del Parlament. La plataforma ha advertit que “ no n’hi ha prou amb prohibir els telèfons mòbils als instituts” i ha reclamat una revisió “immediata” de tots els dispositius digitals que Educació proporciona a l’alumnat. articles.body: Barcelona ha assolit el compromís de dedicar un carrer de la ciutat a Arcadi Oliveres , que va ser un reconegut economista i activista en defensa de la justícia social. Així ho ha acordat la Comissió de Drets Socials d’aquest mes d’octubre, a instàncies dels comuns. La proposta ha rebut el sí de BComú , de Junts , del PSC i d’ ERC . Arcadi Oliveres va morir l’abril del 2021 , als 75 anys, i un parell d’anys abans va rebre la Medalla d’Or al Mèrit Cívic de l’Ajuntament de Barcelona, per la seva trajectòria en defensa de la pau , el desarmament i els drets humans . Per a aquesta trajectòria, Jordi Rabassa (BComú) ha dit en comissió que “Barcelona ha de ser una ciutat que aposti pels valors que defensava Oliveres”. Els comuns demanen que el carrer dedicat sigui a l’Eixample o a Sarrià – Sant Gervasi . articles.body: Aquesta matinada ens ha deixat als 95 anys Pere Ferré i Balasch (1931, Cornellà de Llobregat) , pianista de jazz de llarguíssima trajectòria i història viva del gènere al nostre país. Ferré va cursar estudis de piano al Conservatori Municipal de Música de Barcelona i va oferir les primeres actuacions a sales de l’època com Saratoga, Arizona i Embassy. La primera gran experiència professional va arribar a principis dels anys 50, quan va substituir el seu amic Tete Montoliu per formar part del Latin Quartet , amb el qual va anar de gira uns dos anys per Holanda, Alemanya i Escandinàvia. A les dècades dels anys 60 i 70 va establir una forta vinculació amb l’escena jazzística vallesana amb epicentre, a partir del 1971, a la Jazz Cava de Terrassa. Hi va oficiar amb el Modern Jazz Quintet (amb Josep M. Farràs, Vicens Vacca, Salvador Vila i Adrià Font). Com a líder del seu trio va actuar a la sala en la dècada dels anys 70 i 80, en plena expansió de la sala egarenca. També et pot interessar Pere Ferré, pianista: “Tinc memoritzats més de 500 temes” Víctor Giralt Jonama 2 minuts de lectura Amb figures internacionals Ferré va actuar en festivals de jazz a Donostia, Victòria, Granada, Sevilla, València, Màlaga i Barcelona i va acompanyar coneguts músics de l’escena internacional en les seves visites al país, com els trompetistes Bill Coleman i Ed Kleiger ; els saxofonistes Guy Lafitte , Pony Poindexter , Earle Warren i Billy Mitchell i el trombonista Gene “Mighty Fle” Conners, entre molt d’altres. En la darrera etapa de la seva vida va actuar amb regularitat a restaurants com el 7 Portes i el Giardinetto. Darrerament també se’l va poder escoltar mensualment al Jazzman amb la formació The Jazzman Quartet. Només va enregistrar un únic disc com a líder, Secret love , amb Horacio Fumero i Peer Wyboris (Fresh Sound Records, 2001).
